title: Hip osteoarthritis and frailty: turning in bed and getting up (UK)

direct_answer: With hip osteoarthritis and frailty, turning in bed and getting up are usually easier if you roll as one unit, use your arms and a firm mattress edge, and get up in stages. Bed height, a bed lever fitted after an occupational therapy assessment, and a clear, lit route to the toilet all help.

content:
Turning over and getting out of bed can become one of the hardest parts of the day with hip osteoarthritis, especially if you are also frail. Hips are often stiffest after lying still, and weaker leg and arm muscles make it harder to push yourself up. Rolling as one unit, getting up in stages, the right bed height and simple equipment can make it safer and less painful.

This guide covers turning in bed, sitting up, standing up from the bed, and night-time safety. It is educational information; if a physiotherapist or occupational therapist has given you a plan, follow that first.

Why beds get harder with hip osteoarthritis and frailty

Hip osteoarthritis can cause stiffness after rest, pain when you lie on the affected side, and difficulty bending the hip. Frailty adds weaker muscles, slower recovery and a higher risk of falls. Together, they can turn getting out of bed into a big effort, and some people start sleeping in a chair to avoid it. That can make stiffness and swollen ankles worse, so it is worth getting help early.

Turning over in bed

  • Bend your knees one at a time, keeping your feet flat on the bed.
  • Turn your head and reach your arm across in the direction you want to roll.
  • Let your knees fall to that side together, and roll your shoulders and hips as one unit rather than twisting.
  • A pillow between your knees can make lying on your side more comfortable.
  • Satin sheets or a slide sheet can reduce friction. Ask an occupational therapist before using a slide sheet, as it can make the bed slippery when getting out.

Getting from lying to sitting

  • Roll onto your side, facing the edge you get out from.
  • Let your lower legs slide over the edge of the bed.
  • At the same time, push up with your lower elbow and then your upper hand to bring your body upright.
  • Sit for a moment before standing. Feeling dizzy when you sit up is common, especially with some blood pressure medicines; wait until it settles.

Standing up from the bed

  • Shuffle forward so you are sitting near the edge, with your feet flat on the floor and slightly apart.
  • Lean forward, "nose over toes", and push up through your hands on the bed rather than pulling on a walking frame.
  • Stand still for a few seconds and check your balance before walking.
  • If you use a walking aid, keep it within reach of the bed.

Getting the bed height right

A bed that is too low makes standing up much harder for painful hips. A bed that is too high can make it hard to get your feet on the floor. A rough guide is that when you sit on the edge, your hips should be level with or slightly higher than your knees and your feet flat on the floor. Bed raisers, a firmer mattress or a different bed may help. An occupational therapist can measure this for you.

Bed levers and other equipment

A bed lever (sometimes called a bed stick) gives you something firm to hold when you roll or sit up. Some types are not safe for every bed or person, as gaps between the rail and the mattress can cause entrapment, so ask for an occupational therapy assessment first. Equipment is often loaned free through community equipment services after an assessment. Other helpful items include a leg lifter, a bed raiser and a grab rail near the bed.

Night-time safety

Many falls happen on the way to the toilet at night. Keep a light within reach of the bed, use night lights on the route, keep the floor clear, and wear well-fitting slippers or shoes. If you get up several times a night, a commode or urinal by the bed may help, and it is worth telling your GP, as night toilet trips can have treatable causes.

Easing night pain and morning stiffness

NICE recommends exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis. Gentle hip movements such as knee rolls or heel slides before getting up can ease stiffness. A warm, not hot, shower in the morning may help. If pain wakes you most nights, ask your GP for a review of your pain treatment rather than increasing painkillers yourself.

When to get help

  • Call 999 after a fall if you may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip, or cannot get up, or if your leg looks shortened or turned out.
  • Get urgent advice the same day if your hip suddenly becomes much more painful or you cannot put weight on it, or if you have a hot, swollen joint with a fever.
  • See your GP if getting out of bed is getting harder week by week, if pain stops you sleeping, or if you have had a fall.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Should I sleep in a chair instead?

It can feel easier, but sleeping in a chair long term can make stiffness, swollen legs and skin problems worse. Ask for an occupational therapy assessment of your bed and equipment instead.

Which side should I get out of bed?

Many people find it easier to lead with their less painful leg. An occupational therapist or physiotherapist can help you work out what suits you.

Can I get equipment free?

Often, yes, after an assessment. Ask your GP for a referral or contact your council for a care needs assessment.
